title: Move commits with no network at all
summary: An air-gapped machine, a locked-down customer site, a flaky VPN. git bundle packages commits into a single file you can carry on a USB stick, and it behaves exactly like a remote.
mental_model: A bundle is a packfile plus a list of refs, in one file. Git can clone from it, fetch from it, and list its refs — everything it does with a URL, because a bundle is just a remote that happens to be a file.

steps.title: Package the whole repository into one file
steps.why: `--all` bundles every ref. The result is a single file containing the complete history — a backup you can email, burn to a disc, or carry through a security door.
steps.expect: One file, and a list of the refs inside it including the tag.

verify.label: the bundle contains the main branch

steps.title: Verify it before trusting it
steps.why: `bundle verify` checks the packfile is intact and reports which commits the receiving repository must already have. For a full bundle the answer is none — it is self-contained.
steps.expect: 'The bundle records a complete history' — no prerequisites.

steps.title: Clone from the file, as if it were a server
steps.why: This is the part that surprises people: a bundle is a valid clone URL. The clone has full history, tags and a working tree, with no network involved at any point.
steps.expect: Three commits, the v1.0 tag, and the files — from a single file.

verify.label: a full clone was made from the bundle file

steps.title: Work happens on both sides
steps.why: The two repositories now diverge with no way to talk to each other. Everything below is the offline equivalent of push and pull.

actions.run: git commit -q -a -m "Alert on pH drift too"

steps.title: Bundle only what is new
steps.why: A full bundle of a large repository is huge. Naming a range — `v1.0..main` — produces an incremental bundle containing only the new commits, with v1.0 recorded as a prerequisite.
steps.expect: A much smaller file, and verify reporting that the receiver needs the v1.0 commit already.

steps.title: Apply the update on the other side
steps.why: `git fetch <bundle> <refspec>` treats the file as a remote. Because the airgapped clone already has v1.0, the prerequisite is satisfied and the new commits apply.
steps.expect: Five commits on the airgapped side, fetched from a file.

verify.label: the incremental bundle brought the new commits across
…and the files that came with them

steps.title: Send work back the same way
steps.why: Bundles are symmetric. The isolated machine commits, bundles its range, and the file travels back — a complete two-way workflow with no network on either side.

steps.expect: The site's commit merged back, having travelled as a file.

verify.label: the offline machine's work came back the same way
…including its files
verify.hint: git bundle create <file> <range>, then fetch from it

steps.title: Use it as a backup you can actually restore
steps.why: One file, verifiable, restorable with `git clone`. Unlike a tarball of the working tree it contains the full history — and unlike a hosted mirror it needs no service to stay alive.
commands: sh -c 'git bundle create ../reef-backup.bundle --all && git bundle verify ../reef-backup.bundle | tail -2'
sh -c 'git clone -q ../reef-backup.bundle ../restored && cd ../restored && git log --oneline | wc -l'

verify.label: the backup bundle restores the complete history
work travelled both ways with no network
verify.hint: bundle a range, fetch from the file, merge

verify.label: the offline clone received the update bundle

pitfalls: An incremental bundle records prerequisites. If the receiving repository lacks them, the fetch fails — `git bundle verify` tells you before you carry the file across the building.
`git bundle create <file> --all` bundles every ref including remote-tracking ones. Use explicit refs when you want a tidy handover.
A bundle is a snapshot. Nothing updates it, so a bundle used as a backup is only as fresh as the day you made it.
Cloning from a bundle sets the bundle file as `origin`. Repoint the remote afterwards, or the first `git fetch` looks for a file that has been deleted.
Bundles are not encrypted or signed. Anything sensitive needs handling at the file level.
cheatsheet: the whole repository in one file
